messages.content: Classical entry: 甘草 (Glycyrrhiza uralensis / G. glabra), root; 性味歸經: 甘, 平; 歸心、肺、脾、胃經; 上品. Known constituents: glycyrrhizin (glycyrrhizic acid), glycyrrhetinic acid, liquiritin, isoliquiritigenin. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: triterpenoid saponin (oleanane). Candidate molecule: 18beta-glycyrrhetinic acid (the aglycone of glycyrrhizin, formed by gut bacterial beta-glucuronidase). Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (HSD11B2) in kidney, raising local cortisol and producing mineralocorticoid-like effects; a second, independent hypothesis is direct mineralocorticoid receptor modulation. Asian-theory justification: 甘 (sweet) and 平 (neutral) are the classical descriptors of a harmonising, qi-supplementing drug, and the channel tropism to 脾/胃 is consistent with an adrenal-steroid mechanism, but the mapping is post-hoc and must not be treated as evidence. Assay: HSD11B2 activity in transfected HEK293 cells (cortisol-to-cortisone conversion by LC-MS); specificity against HSD11B1; ex vivo urinary cortisol/cortisone ratio in a controlled animal model. Falsification: if purified 18beta-glycyrrhetinic acid does not shift the cortisol/cortisone ratio at non-cytotoxic concentrations, and HSD11B2 is not inhibited in the cell assay, the hypothesis is dead. Risk: HSD11B2 inhibition is the documented mechanism of licorice-induced pseudohyperaldosteronism, so this is a toxicity liability as much as a lead. This is a mechanistic hypothesis, not evidence of efficacy, and is not dosing advice.
Classical entry: 黃芩 (Scutellaria baicalensis), root; 性味歸經: 苦, 寒; 歸肺、膽、脾、大腸經. Known constituents: baicalin, baicalein, wogonin, oroxylin A. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: flavone (flavonoid). Candidate molecule: baicalein (aglycone of baicalin, liberated by gut glucuronidases). Mechanism hypothesis: 12/15-lipoxygenase (ALOX15) inhibition, reducing inflammatory eicosanoid flux; a competing hypothesis is inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Asian-theory justification: 苦寒 drugs are classically assigned to 'clear heat and dry dampness' - an inflammatory-resolution reading; the 肺/大腸 tropism is consistent with a mucosal-inflammation hypothesis, but the theory-to-mechanism link is interpretive. Assay: purified ALOX15 enzyme inhibition with a fluorescent oxygraphic/LC-MS readout of 12-HETE; selectivity panel against 5-LOX and COX-1/2; LPS-stimulated macrophage IL-1beta readout for the NLRP3 arm. Falsification: no ALOX15 inhibition and no reduction of 12-HETE in cells at sub-cytotoxic doses kills the lipoxygenase hypothesis; the inflammasome hypothesis then requires a separate ASC-speck assay. Risk: baicalein is a known pan-assay-interference risk (redox-active flavonoid), so orthogonal assays with detergent and catalase controls are mandatory.
Classical entry: 青蒿 (Artemisia annua), aerial parts; 性味歸經: 苦、辛, 寒; 歸肝、膽經. Known constituents: artemisinin (qinghaosu), arteannuin B, artemisinic acid. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: sesquiterpene lactone with an endoperoxide bridge. Candidate molecule: artemisinin (and its semi-synthetic derivatives). Mechanism hypothesis: iron(II)- or heme-dependent reductive cleavage of the endoperoxide generates carbon-centred radicals that alkylate multiple parasite proteins; deliberate promiscuity rather than a single target. Asian-theory justification: 苦寒 and 肝/膽 tropism is at best a weak analogue of an antiparasitic hepatic-stage action; the text does not encode the mechanism. Assay: parasite viability in Plasmodium falciparum culture with IC50, plus a matched mammalian cytotoxicity counter-screen; heme-dependence tested by iron chelation and by comparing wild-type to a ferrochelatase-impaired parasite line. Falsification: loss of potency under iron chelation, or no radical-adduct formation on protein electrophoresis, would refute the iron-activation mechanism. Risk: artemisinin resistance in Southeast Asia means candidate novelty must be assessed against existing ACT therapy; do not frame this as a new treatment. No dosing guidance is to be inferred.

Classical entry: 附子 (Aconitum carmichaelii), lateral root, 炮制 required; 性味歸經: 辛, 大熱, 有毒; 歸心、腎、脾經. Known constituents: aconitine, mesaconitine, hypaconitine, plus processed derivatives. Propose a candidate; the toxicity is the point.

Chemotype: diterpene alkaloid (C19-norditerpenoid). Candidate framework: not aconitine itself as a drug lead - its sodium-channel activator liability is the documented cause of fatal arrhythmia. The interesting scientific object is the 炮制 (processing) step, which hydrolyses acetyl/benzoyl esters to far less toxic and far less active products. Mechanism hypothesis: processing converts diester alkaloids to mono- and un-esterified forms, reducing Nav-channel persistent-current activation; residual activity may be anti-inflammatory via a separate, non-Nav route. Asian-theory justification: 大熱 + 有毒 is the classical encoding of a high-potency, high-risk drug that is 'made safe by preparation' - directly testable, unlike most property claims. Assay: whole-cell patch clamp on Nav1.5/Nav1.7 expressing cells for the processed vs unprocessed alkaloid fraction; hERG counter-screen; mouse arrhythmia model only under ethics approval. Falsification: if processing does not reduce persistent-current activation or arrhythmia liability in a dose-matched comparison, the processing-as-detoxification hypothesis fails. Safety: absolute prohibition on any extraction, concentration or dosing guidance; this entry is a toxicology and processing-science case study, not a therapeutic candidate.

Classical entry: 大黃 (Rheum palmatum / R. officinale), root and rhizome; 性味歸經: 苦, 寒; 歸脾、胃、大腸、肝、心包經. Known constituents: emodin, rhein, aloe-emodin, sennosides, chrysophanol. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: anthraquinone / anthrone glycoside. Candidate molecule: rhein (aglycone). Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of the mitochondrial electron-transport chain at complex I/III generating ROS, and separate inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome; the classic laxative effect is a colonic epithelial/secretagogue mechanism that must be separated from the anti-inflammatory hypothesis. Asian-theory justification: 苦寒 purgatives are classically directed at 大腸; attributing the anti-inflammatory action to the same tropism is a modern reading. Assay: Seahorse/respirometry for mitochondrial respiration, LPS-primed THP-1 IL-1beta for NLRP3, and a colonic epithelial secretion assay; anthraquinone redox-cycling controls (detergent, catalase, SOD) are essential. Falsification: loss of IL-1beta suppression under mitochondrial-respiration rescue would argue against an ROS-driven NLRP3 mechanism. Risk: anthraquinones carry genotoxicity and melanosis coli concerns; long-term use signal must be reported, and no dosing is implied.
Classical entry: 黃連 (Coptis chinensis), rhizome; 性味歸經: 苦, 寒; 歸心、脾、胃、肝、膽、大腸經. Known constituents: berberine, coptisine, palmatine, jatrorrhizine. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: protoberberine isoquinoline alkaloid. Candidate molecule: berberine. Mechanism hypothesis: activation of AMPK via mitochondrial respiratory-chain inhibition (increased AMP/ATP), with a secondary hypothesis of gut-microbiota-mediated metabolic effects; the very low oral bioavailability of berberine makes a systemic-intact-drug story implausible, so a gut-lumen mechanism deserves priority. Asian-theory justification: 苦寒 + 大腸 tropism is consistent with a lumenal/microbial mechanism, one of the better-matched theory-to-pharmacology mappings in this corpus. Assay: AMPK Thr172 phosphorylation in HepG2/C2C12, oxygen-consumption rate, and a faecal-microbiota transplant arm in a diet-induced model; germ-free vs colonised comparison to test sufficiency. Falsification: if AMPK activation is abolished in cells lacking a functional respiratory chain, or if no microbiota-dependence is observed, the two hypotheses respectively fail. Risk: berberine inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, so herb-drug interaction potential must be screened; no dosing advice.

Classical entry: 丹參 (Salvia miltiorrhiza), root; 性味歸經: 苦, 微寒; 歸心、肝經. Known constituents: tanshinone I, tanshinone IIA, cryptotanshinone, salvianolic acid B, danshensu. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: abietane diterpene quinone (tanshinones) plus phenolic acids (salvianolic acids). Candidate molecule: tanshinone IIA. Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of the PI3K/AKT survival axis and of STAT3 in vascular smooth-muscle and endothelial cells, with a parallel anti-inflammatory hypothesis via NF-kappaB; the 'invigorate blood' classical action is the analogue being probed. Asian-theory justification: 心/肝 tropism maps to a cardiovascular hypothesis; these tanshinones are lipophilic redox-active quinones. Assay: endothelial tube formation and VSMC proliferation, AKT/STAT3 phosphorylation, and a zebrafish or aortic-ring model; redox-cycling controls are mandatory because quinones are classic assay interferers. Falsification: no reduction of AKT/STAT3 phosphorylation at non-cytotoxic concentrations, or effect disappearing with NQO1 inhibition, weakens the mechanism claim. Risk: tanshinones are CYP substrates/inhibitors and have documented herb-drug interaction signals with warfarin; report as a research lead only.
Classical entry: 麻黃 (Ephedra sinica), stem; 性味歸經: 辛、微苦, 溫; 歸肺、膀胱經. Known constituents: ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, methylephedrine. Propose a candidate and state why this one is a cautionary case.

Chemotype: phenethylamine alkaloid. Candidate molecule: ephedrine. Mechanism hypothesis: mixed-acting sympathomimetic - direct alpha/beta-adrenergic agonism plus noradrenaline release - giving bronchodilatation and pressor effects. Asian-theory justification: 辛溫 + 肺 tropism is a good descriptor of a bronchodilator/sweat-inducing drug, which is why ephedrine was successfully extracted from this plant in 1885 and became a real drug. Assay: beta2-adrenergic cAMP reporter, isolated tracheal-ring relaxation, and a cardiovascular pressor counter-screen; the mechanism is already established, so the research question is selectivity, not discovery. Falsification: the sympathomimetic mechanism is falsified only by showing the effect is not blocked by adrenergic antagonists - unlikely. Risk and judgement: this is the clearest example in the corpus of a classical text encoding a genuine active principle, and simultaneously a case where the isolated alkaloid became a public-health problem (cardiovascular and psychiatric adverse events). Do not propose as a novel lead; it is a textbook and a warning.
Classical entry: 苦參 (Sophora flavescens), root; 性味歸經: 苦, 寒; 歸心、肝、胃、大腸、膀胱經. Known constituents: matrine, oxymatrine, sophoridine, sophocarpine. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: quinolizidine alkaloid. Candidate molecule: oxymatrine (or its metabolite matrine). Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of the TLR4/NF-kappaB and JAK/STAT pathways in activated immune cells, giving an anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic signal (hepatic stellate cell activation is the classical test case). Asian-theory justification: 苦寒 + 肝 tropism supports a hepatic anti-inflammatory hypothesis, which happens to match the modern use of oxymatrine in hepatitis trials in China. Assay: hepatic stellate-cell (LX-2) alpha-SMA and collagen-I readout, TLR4/NF-kappaB luciferase, and a CCl4 or bile-duct-ligation fibrosis model; hepatocyte cytotoxicity must be measured in parallel. Falsification: no reduction of alpha-SMA/collagen at non-cytotoxic doses, or effect only at concentrations above cytotoxicity, kills the anti-fibrotic claim. Risk: quinolizidine alkaloids have neurotoxicity signals at high exposure; the exposure window is narrow and must be reported.

Classical entry: 白芍 (Paeonia lactiflora), root; 性味歸經: 苦、酸, 微寒; 歸肝、脾經. Known constituents: paeoniflorin, albiflorin, paeonol (in some species), benzoyl-paeoniflorin. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: monoterpene glycoside (pinane skeleton). Candidate molecule: paeoniflorin. Mechanism hypothesis: modulation of the adenosine A1 receptor and of smooth-muscle calcium handling, producing spasmolytic and analgesic effects; a secondary hypothesis is inhibition of inflammatory NF-kappaB signalling. Asian-theory justification: 酸 (astringent) and 肝 tropism fit the classical 'soften the liver and relieve pain' description, which is unusually close to a smooth-muscle/analgesic hypothesis. Assay: A1 receptor radioligand binding and cAMP readout, isolated ileum/uterine smooth-muscle contractility, and a capsaicin/formal test for analgesia; paeoniflorin is poorly bioavailable and the aglycone is the relevant species, so metabolite testing is needed. Falsification: no A1 binding and no spasmolytic effect at achievable exposures kills the mechanism claim; an effect that persists in A1-knockout tissue refutes the receptor hypothesis. Risk: low acute toxicity signal but bioavailability is the main drug-development obstacle.
Classical entry: 陳皮 (Citrus reticulata), aged pericarp; 性味歸經: 辛、苦, 溫; 歸肺、脾經. Known constituents: hesperidin, nobiletin, tangeretin, limonene. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: flavanone glycoside (hesperidin/hesperetin) and polymethoxyflavones (nobiletin, tangeretin). Candidate molecule: nobiletin. Mechanism hypothesis: circadian-clock modulation (RORalpha/REV-ERB) plus AMPK activation, giving metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects; a separate hypothesis is intestinal barrier and anti-emetic actions for the classical digestive use. Asian-theory justification: 辛温 + 肺/脾 tropism supports an airway-and-digestion hypothesis, which is the same axis modern studies of polymethoxyflavones explore. Assay: circadian reporter (Bmal1-luc) amplitude/phase shift, RORalpha binding, metabolic phenotyping in diet-induced obesity, and an intestinal barrier (TEER) assay; polymethoxyflavones are pan-assay-interference-prone and require orthogonal controls. Falsification: no phase shift of the circadian reporter in RORalpha-null cells refutes the clock hypothesis; no TEER protection argues against the barrier hypothesis. Risk: citrus polymethoxyflavones inhibit CYP3A4 in vitro; interaction risk must be screened.

Classical entry: 生薑 (Zingiber officinale), fresh rhizome; 性味歸經: 辛, 微溫; 歸肺、脾、胃經. Known constituents: 6-gingerol, 6-shogaol, zingerone, gingerols, terpenes. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: phenolic alkanone (gingerol class). Candidate molecule: 6-shogaol (dehydration product of 6-gingerol, enriched by drying/processing). Mechanism hypothesis: TRPV1 agonism and 5-HT3 receptor antagonism, giving the documented anti-emetic and GI-prokinetic effects; a secondary hypothesis is covalent Nrf2 activation by the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone. Asian-theory justification: 辛温 + 脾胃 tropism and the classical use for nausea map unusually directly onto a 5-HT3/TRPV1 hypothesis; the processing step (drying) genuinely changes the constituent profile, which is a testable 'processing as chemistry' case. Assay: TRPV1 calcium flux, 5-HT3 radioligand binding, and an emesis model (ferret or conditioned taste-aversion) alongside a Nrf2 reporter; 6-shogaol reactivity requires thiol-adduct controls. Falsification: no 5-HT3 binding and no emesis reduction in a validated model kills the anti-emetic mechanism claim. Risk: TRPV1 agonism can cause GI irritation; no dosing advice.

Classical entry: 五味子 (Schisandra chinensis), fruit; 性味歸經: 酸、甘, 溫; 歸肺、心、腎經. Known constituents: schisandrin (schizandrin), schisandrol A/B, gomisin A, deoxyschizandrin. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: dibenzocyclooctadiene lignan. Candidate molecule: schisandrin (schizandrol). Mechanism hypothesis: activation of the Nrf2/ARE antioxidant program and inhibition of CYP3A4/P-gp, i.e. a 'hepatoprotective plus pharmacokinetic-modifier' duality; the two effects must be separated because one is a benefit hypothesis and the other is a drug-interaction liability. Asian-theory justification: 酸收 + 肺/心/腎 tropism is a classical descriptor of an 'astringent, qi-gathering' drug; the Nrf2 reading is a modern reinterpretation, not something the text encodes. Assay: Nrf2/ARE luciferase, HO-1 induction in hepatocytes, and a CYP3A4 midazolam hydroxylation assay plus P-gp efflux; a rodent pharmacokinetic interaction study with a marker substrate. Falsification: no ARE induction in Nrf2-knockout cells refutes the antioxidant hypothesis; no shift in midazolam PK refutes the CYP claim. Risk: the CYP/P-gp inhibition is a real herb-drug interaction risk and should be reported as a safety signal.

Classical entry: 天麻 (Gastrodia elata), tuber; 性味歸經: 甘, 平; 歸肝經. Known constituents: gastrodin, gastrodigenin (p-hydroxybenzyl alcohol), parishin, vanillyl alcohol. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: phenolic glucoside. Candidate molecule: gastrodin (and its aglycone gastrodigenin after hydrolysis). Mechanism hypothesis: GABAergic/glutamatergic modulation - weak GABA-A potentiation and reduced presynaptic glutamate release - giving anticonvulsant and neuroprotective effects; a secondary hypothesis is inhibition of microglial inflammatory activation. Asian-theory justification: 甘平 + 肝 tropism and the classical use for 'extinguishing wind and stopping tremors' is a remarkably direct description of an anticonvulsant/antispastic action; it is one of the better theory matches in the corpus. Assay: patch-clamp GABA-A currents, hippocampal slice seizure-like activity (high-K or 4-AP), and a maximal-electroshock seizure model; gastrodin's low CNS penetration must be measured (brain/plasma ratio) because it constrains the hypothesis. Falsification: no brain exposure above the effective in vitro concentration, or no effect on 4-AP bursting, kills the central mechanism claim. Risk: low toxicity signal, but brain penetration is the likely development blocker.
Classical entry: 柴胡 (Bupleurum chinense), root; 性味歸經: 苦、辛, 微寒; 歸肝、膽經. Known constituents: saikosaponin A, saikosaponin D, bupleurumol, ferulic acid. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin. Candidate molecule: saikosaponin D (and its aglycone saikogenin after hydrolysis). Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of NF-kappaB and of the NLRP3 inflammasome, plus a membrane-permeabilising effect that can be cytotoxic at higher concentrations; the therapeutic window is therefore central to the claim. Asian-theory justification: 苦辛微寒 + 肝/膽 tropism maps onto the classical 'harmonise shaoyang' use, which modern work interprets as anti-inflammatory. Assay: NF-kappaB luciferase, IL-1beta ELISA in LPS-primed macrophages, LDH release for membrane toxicity, and a hepatic injury model; the saponin's surfactant-like activity demands a critical-micelle-concentration control. Falsification: if the anti-inflammatory effect only appears at concentrations that also cause LDH release, the claim is cytotoxicity, not modulation, and is refuted. Risk: saponin haemolysis and hepatotoxicity signals at high dose; no dosing is implied.

Classical entry: Aśvagandhā (Withania somnifera), root; rasa: tikta, kaṣāya; guṇa: laghu, snigdha; vīrya: uṣṇa; vipāka: madhura; doṣa: vāta-kapha pacifying. Known constituents: withaferin A, withanolide D, withanoside IV, sitoindosides. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: withanolide (ergostane-type steroidal lactone). Candidate molecule: withaferin A. Mechanism hypothesis: covalent modification of the IKKbeta cysteine, inhibiting NF-kappaB, plus vimentin/heat-shock-protein interactions; a second hypothesis concerns GABA-mimetic activity of withanosides for the classical 'calming' use. Asian-theory justification: uṣṇa vīrya (hot potency) and vāta-pacifying action are a classical prediction about neuro/immune effects; treating it as a mechanistic claim is exactly the kind of test the project wants, not an assumption. Assay: NF-kappaB luciferase with a cysteine-reactivity control, IKKbeta labelling, GABA-A current recording, and a stress/behaviour readout only under ethics approval; withaferin A is highly reactive and cell-type toxicity must be mapped. Falsification: no NF-kappaB inhibition in IKKbeta-Cys179 mutant cells refutes the covalent mechanism; no GABA current modulation refutes the sedative hypothesis. Risk: withaferin A is cytotoxic and anti-proliferative - a potential lead and a potential hazard; not a supplement recommendation.

Classical entry: Triphalā - Harītakī (Terminalia chebula), Bibhītaka (Terminalia bellirica), Āmalakī (Phyllanthus emblica), fruit. Known constituents: chebulinic acid, chebulagic acid, gallic/ellagic acid, emblicanin A/B, vitamin C. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: hydrolysable tannins (gallotannins and ellagitannins). Candidate molecule: chebulinic acid (and ellagic acid as the gut-liberated aglycone). Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of SARS-CoV 3CL protease and of HIV-1 integrase has been reported for these tannins in vitro, while a more plausible physiological effect is gut-microbiota modulation and metal chelation; the chemical reactivity (protein binding, chelation) is also the likely source of assay artefacts. Asian-theory justification: Triphalā's classical action is tridoṣa-balancing and gentle cleansing, which does not encode a target; the honest position is that no mechanistic claim is warranted from the theory. Assay: 3CL protease FRET assay with detergent/tannin controls, integrase strand-transfer assay, faecal microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid output, and a metal-chelation counter-screen. Falsification: if activity in the protease assay disappears when the enzyme is pre-incubated with a non-ionic detergent that blocks promiscuous tannin binding, the specific-inhibition claim is refuted. Risk: tannins bind proteins non-specifically and can impair iron absorption; no therapeutic claim.

Classical entry: Brāhmī (Bacopa monnieri), whole plant; rasa: tikta, kaṣāya; vīrya: uṣṇa (some texts: śīta); doṣa: vāta-kapha pacifying, pitta-increasing. Known constituents: bacoside A3, bacopaside I/II, bacopasaponin C, hersaponin. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: dammarane-type triterpenoid saponin (jujubogenin and pseudojujubogenin glycosides). Candidate molecule: bacoside A3. Mechanism hypothesis: enhancement of hippocampal synaptic plasticity via BDNF/TrkB and NMDA-receptor signalling, with a secondary hypothesis of antioxidant/adaptogenic action; the classical 'medhya' (intellect-promoting) description is the hypothesis being tested, and it is testable in LTP and memory paradigms. Asian-theory justification: the medhya claim is a functional, not a humoral, claim and can be operationalised as a plasticity endpoint; that makes it one of the more falsifiable Ayurvedic claims. Assay: hippocampal LTP in slices, BDNF/TrkB phosphorylation, and a Morris-water-maze or novel-object test under ethics approval; bacoside brain exposure must be measured because saponin CNS penetration is the weak link. Falsification: absence of LTP enhancement at brain concentrations reached after oral administration kills the mechanism claim, even if in vitro activity exists. Risk: GI upset is reported; bacosides can be haemolytic. No dosing advice.

Classical entry: Haridrā (Curcuma longa), rhizome; rasa: tikta, kaṭu; vīrya: uṣṇa; doṣa: kapha-vāta pacifying, pitta-increasing. Known constituents: curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, bisdemethoxycurcumin, turmerone. Propose a candidate and be explicit about the known bioavailability problem.

Chemotype: curcuminoid (diarylheptanoid). Candidate molecule: curcumin. Mechanism hypothesis: a very long list of reported targets (NF-kappaB, STAT3, Nrf2, amyloid aggregation, IKK) that has not produced an approved drug; the most defensible current hypothesis is a reactive, aggregation-prone electrophile that covalently modifies many proteins, i.e. promiscuous rather than selective. Asian-theory justification: uṣṇa vīrya and pitta-increasing are classical process descriptors, not target predictions; no mechanistic claim should be drawn from them. Assay: before target claims, run PAINS/assay-interference controls (detergent, catalase, thiol-adduct), soluble vs aggregated curcumin characterisation, and a pharmacokinetic study with a validated plasma assay; a target hypothesis is only worth testing once free tissue concentrations are demonstrated. Falsification: if the reported in vitro activity is abolished by detergent or by using a curcumin analogue that does not aggregate, the target-specific claim is refuted. Risk: curcumin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp in vitro and can potentiate anticoagulants; the honest conclusion is a cautionary case study about a famous natural product with weak translation.

Classical entry: 茯苓 (Poria cocos), sclerotium; 性味歸經: 甘、淡, 平; 歸心、肺、脾、腎經. Known constituents: pachymic acid, poricoic acid, lanostane triterpenes, polysaccharides. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay.

Chemotype: lanostane triterpenoid. Candidate molecule: pachymic acid. Mechanism hypothesis: modulation of the glucocorticoid receptor and of the NLRP3 inflammasome, with an independent polysaccharide-driven immunomodulation hypothesis (the two must be assayed as separate chemical fractions). Asian-theory justification: 甘淡 (sweet, bland) + 水-channeling classical action is a diuretic/mucosal-transport descriptor; a mineralocorticoid-receptor or renal-transport hypothesis is the modern translation and is testable. Assay: GR transactivation reporter, NLRP3 IL-1beta assay, and a renal sodium/water handling study with fractionation; the polysaccharide fraction needs an endotoxin-controlled preparation because TLR4 readouts are notoriously contaminated. Falsification: no GR transactivation and no renal transport effect for purified pachymic acid kills the triterpenoid hypothesis; a TLR4 response that disappears after polymyxin B treatment was endotoxin, not polysaccharide. Risk: low toxicity; polysaccharide fractions are the usual assay-artefact trap.

Classical entry: 何首烏 (Polygonum multiflorum / Reynoutria multiflora), root, processed (製何首烏); 性味歸經: 苦、甘、澀, 微溫; 歸肝、心、腎經. Known constituents: emodin, physcion, 2,3,5,4'-tetrahydroxystilbene-2-O-beta-D-glucoside (TSG), catechin. Propose a candidate and address the hepatotoxicity signal explicitly.

Chemotype: stilbene glycoside (TSG) plus anthraquinones (emodin, physcion). Candidate molecule: TSG as the claimed active, emodin as the leading toxicity candidate. Mechanism hypothesis: TSG has reported antioxidant and neuroprotective effects, while the idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity signal is plausibly driven by anthraquinones plus metabolic activation and immune-mediated injury; the two hypotheses are chemically separable and that is the experiment. Asian-theory justification: processing with black bean juice (九蒸九晒) is classically said to 'remove toxicity and enhance tonification' - a directly testable processing-as-detoxification claim, and one with real clinical relevance. Assay: comparative hepatotoxicity of processed vs unprocessed fractions in primary human hepatocytes with CYP3A4/UGT phenotyping, plus metabolomics for reactive intermediates; TSG and emodin quantified in both fractions. Falsification: if processing does not reduce anthraquinone content or cytotoxicity, the classical processing rationale is falsified; if cytotoxicity is TSG-independent, the emodin hypothesis gains support. Safety: this plant has a documented drug-induced liver injury signal; no dosing or self-use guidance, and the honest output is a toxicity warning, not a recommendation.

Classical entry: Afsantīn (Artemisia absinthium) described in the Unani canon with hot-dry temperament and use in hepatic and gastric complaints. Known constituents: absinthin, artabsin, thujone, chamazulene. Propose a candidate with mechanism and assay, and note the difference from the Asian Artemisia.

Chemotype: sesquiterpene lactone (guaianolide) plus monoterpene ketones. Candidate molecule: absinthin. Mechanism hypothesis: inhibition of NF-kappaB and of leukotriene biosynthesis (the guaianolide alpha-methylene-gamma-lactone reacts with cysteine thiols), giving an anti-inflammatory and bitter-taste (TAS2R) driven gastric secretion effect. Asian-theory justification: Unani hot-dry temperament with hepatic action is a humoral prediction; the modern translation is choleretic/anti-inflammatory, and the mapping must be labelled interpretive. Assay: NF-kappaB luciferase, 5-LOX product measurement, TAS2R14 activation, and a bile-flow study; thujone content must be quantified and reported because it is the toxicity driver. Falsification: loss of NF-kappaB inhibition in a thiol-reactivity control, or absence of effect on bile flow, respectively refutes the two arms. Safety: thujone is neurotoxic at high exposure - no essential-oil use, no dosing advice. Note: this is a Western/Central-Asian Artemisia, distinct from A. annua; the comparison is taxonomic, not therapeutic.
